Zero (short-run and long-run) restrictions in an A-B / Blanchard-Quah style

Source: R/id-extra.R
id_restrictions.Rd

General exactly- or under-identifying zero pattern on the impact matrix \(P\) (\(u_t=P\varepsilon_t\)) and on the long-run matrix \(\Theta_\infty = (I-\sum A_l)^{-1}P\). Entries equal to 0 are restricted to zero, NA (or anything else) are free. For a just-identified pattern (after ordering shocks by number of zeros the counts are \(K-1,K-2,\dots,0\)) the rotation is unique up to column signs, found in closed form by sequential null-space projections (the ARRW algorithm of id_zerosign(), no numerical optimiser needed), so \(\Sigma=PP'\) and every zero hold to machine precision. Shock signs are normalised so that the impact response of variable j to shock j (or the first free entry of column j) is positive. Over-identified patterns are rejected (more zeros than the counting allows); under-identified patterns give random draws from the admissible set (see the missing-weights note in id_zerosign()).

Usage

id_restrictions(impact = NULL, longrun = NULL)

Arguments

impact, longrun

K x K matrices with 0 for zero restrictions and NA for free elements.

Value

a varm_id object.

Details

Economic intuition. The usual structural-VAR workhorse: Sims' recursive scheme is impact = lower triangular, Blanchard-Quah is longrun = lower triangular, and mixed schemes (e.g. Gali 1992, Blanchard-Perotti with a long-run block) combine both. Pitfall: the zeros are identifying assumptions that cannot be tested in the just-identified case.

See also

Other identification: id_hetero(), id_proxy(), id_zerosign(), identification, irf_fry_pagan(), proxy_draws()

Examples

lower <- matrix(NA, 3, 3)
lower[upper.tri(lower)] <- 0
irf(varm(yraw, p = 2), id_restrictions(impact = lower), 3, ci = "none")
#> <varm IRF> K = 3, horizon 0..3, id = restrictions
#> sign-restriction acceptance rate: 1
